title: Nvidia’s DLSS 5 leak is making games prettier and people weirder

questions.question: By January 31, 2027, will public testing of NVIDIA’s finished DLSS 5 show that it improves game performance rather than imposing a substantial performance penalty?
questions.why_it_matters: DLSS’s appeal depends partly on delivering better visuals without sacrificing performance. If the finished technology carries a large performance cost, that could limit player and game-developer adoption and weaken the competitive value of NVIDIA’s gaming graphics software.
questions.why_not_already_covered: Existing questions track whether NVIDIA launches DLSS 5 and whether it officially supports RTX 40-series GPUs. Neither resolves the separate outcome of DLSS 5’s performance impact in its finished form: the technology could launch and be supported on those GPUs while still imposing a substantial performance penalty.
questions.how_and_when_to_check: Check by January 31, 2027, an analyst check date at NVIDIA’s FY2027 year-end; the article gives no date for final-version performance testing. Review independent benchmarks and testing of the released DLSS 5 in games, comparing performance with and without its neural-rendering features. The article’s reported result is from a leaked, unfinished build, not the final product.

evidence.quote: There is another catch: performance. The leaked build is reportedly extremely resource-intensive. One report cited by XDA says a user running DLSS 5 through a Discord server experienced an almost 50% performance loss. That is a particularly important caveat because DLSS has traditionally been about getting better-looking graphics while improving performance through techniques such as upscaling.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article reports a potentially material performance penalty in an early build and contrasts it with DLSS’s traditional performance-enhancing purpose. The almost 50% loss is attributed to a report cited by XDA, not established as a final-version result.
evidence.original_speaker: Moinak Pal, citing a report by XDA for the user’s reported experience.

evidence.what_it_shows: This qualifies the early performance concern: the software is unfinished, and final implementation or games developed for it could perform better.

evidence.what_it_shows: The article describes a potential efficiency benefit that could offset the reported performance penalty, but presents it as a possibility rather than a demonstrated result.

article:
By Moinak Pal
We all know Nvidia announced its latest DLSS 5 back in March 2026, which promised photorealistic lighting in games. However, Nvidia’s big leap in AI-powered gaming graphics has now arrived unexpectedly: through a leaked, unfinished version of DLSS 5 that modders have already managed to run in several games. The early results are impressive, strange and, in some cases, downright unsettling.
DLSS 5 is expected to take Nvidia’s neural rendering technology further by using generative AI to alter how games look. An early version has now leaked through NBA 2K26’s early access, according to Videocardz . Modders identified an nvngx_dlsrnr.dll library containing an unreleased DLSS Neural Rendering runtime, version 310.8.0.0, and quickly began experimenting with it.
Modders are putting DLSS 5 through some very weird tests
The leaked software has already been made to work with games including Control, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim and Final Fantasy VII Rebirth. There are also examples of the technology being tested with Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas.
And this is where things get interesting. Rather than simply making games sharper, the early implementation appears capable of changing visual details using AI. In Control, the results reportedly do not look particularly bad, especially when it comes to environmental detail. But the technology becomes considerably stranger when applied to characters.
In Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, for example, Cloud’s face can become barely recognizable under the experimental processing. The effect gives some characters an uncanny appearance, suggesting that Nvidia’s generative approach may still have plenty of rough edges to iron out.
There is another catch: performance. The leaked build is reportedly extremely resource-intensive. One report cited by XDA says a user running DLSS 5 through a Discord server experienced an almost 50% performance loss. That is a particularly important caveat because DLSS has traditionally been about getting better-looking graphics while improving performance through techniques such as upscaling.
This may be the future of graphics – or the beginning of AI slop in games
Nvidia has been pitching DLSS 5 as a major evolution of its graphics technology, with CEO Jensen Huang previously pushing back against criticism of the approach. The leaked build gives gamers their first opportunity to see what that generative-AI future might actually look like, although it would be premature to judge the final product from unfinished software.
That distinction matters. We know that this is an unfinished version of DLSS 5, meaning Nvidia could substantially change how it works before release. Games specifically developed around the technology could also produce much better results than older titles being modified by enthusiasts.
Still, the early experiments expose the central challenge Nvidia faces. AI can generate or reconstruct visual information that traditional rendering methods struggle with, but gamers are unlikely to accept sharper graphics if characters suddenly look like digital mannequins.
For Nvidia, DLSS 5 could eventually make games more detailed and visually convincing while reducing the amount of conventional rendering required. For players, however, the question is simpler: will AI make games look better, or merely make them look different? The answer will have to wait for the finished version.
Infinity Ward’s latest campaign goes back to Call of Duty’s roots and recaptures what made me a fan more than a decade ago.
The Call of Duty franchise has held a special place in my heart ever since I played my first Black Ops game back in 2010. That game's campaign was something else, with twists and turns that culminated in a mind-blowing finale. We can all admit that compared to those older campaigns, the recent CODs have been lackluster at best, and a complete and utter disappointment at worst. The reboot of Modern Warfare did give me some hope, as the first two installments were actually quite good, but the third game left such a bad taste in my mouth that I wasn’t exactly expecting much from Modern Warfare 4.
After recently finishing the campaign, I can say that this installment is nothing like the recent releases and instead feels closer to the franchise’s roots. For the first time in a long while, the campaign comes across as well-crafted rather than rushed to hit a release date. It arrives three years after MW3, and you can see exactly where all that time went. It seems the studio finally made listening to player feedback a priority.
Epic Games has just announced the 2026 Epic AI MegaJam, which is looking to see how much game development can be squeezed into a very short window. This is running from November 12 through November 15.
Participants can work alone or in teams of up to five people, build in Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite, and bring along “as many AI agents as you want.” Epic explicitly encourages coding agents, AI-generated assets, audio tools, writing tools, and other AI systems. The official event page literally says "Vibe your way to $50k.”
The free-to-play spin-off launches October 29 with open-world exploration, mobile-focused combat, and a building system.
It’s turning into a pretty good time to be a Monster Hunter fan who plays on a phone. Capcom has confirmed that Monster Hunter Outlanders will launch on Android and iOS on October 29, giving the series a new mobile-first game just as Monster Hunter Rise is also preparing to make the jump to smartphones through Netflix.
Outlanders is being developed by Tencent subsidiary TiMi Studio Group under license and supervision from Capcom. Unlike Rise, which appears to be the full console and PC game adapted for mobile, Outlanders is a free-to-play survival hunting game made specifically for phones.
